speaker: Karina Nguyen
title: The Agent Reasoning Interface: Claude, ChatGPT Canvas, Tasks, Operator — with Karina Nguyen
question: When building a novel AI-native product feature, what are the hardest operational challenges that outside engineers typically underestimate?
guest: It's always hard with any new product feature, like Canvas or Tasks. You don't know how people will use the feature, so how do you even build evaluations that simulate how people will use it? That's always really hard for us, so we lean on iterative deployment to learn from user feedback as much as possible. For example, we didn't know that code diffs were very difficult for a model. So you face decisions: do we go back to fundamentally improve code diffs as a model capability, or do we use a workaround where the model rewrites the entire document, which yields higher accuracy? You have to figure out how to raise product quality while making sure model quality is part of it, and what trade-offs you're okay making. This new way of product development is more like product research, where model training and product development go hand in hand. Defining all the model behaviors is one of the hardest things because so many edge cases happen, especially when you combine Canvas with other tools like DALL-E or search—figuring out which behaviors matter most is how you build evals.

points.core: Teams cannot build realistic pre-launch evaluations before observing how real users interact.
points.note: Accept: unpredictable real-world user behavior prevents fully accurate pre-launch evals, forcing iterative deployment to learn from live feedback. Do not credit: generic advice to 'talk to users'.

points.core: Product teams constantly trade off fundamental model improvements against higher-accuracy product workarounds.
points.note: Accept: choosing between post-training a weak capability (e.g., targeted code diffs) versus engineering a product workaround (e.g., full document rewrites) to meet the quality bar. Do not credit: vague statements about balancing quality and speed.

points.core: Composing a new feature with existing tools creates an explosion of edge cases.
points.note: Accept: cross-feature tool interactions (e.g., combining an editor with search or image generation) multiply behavioral edge cases and force prioritization of what to evaluate. Do not credit: generic statements that edge cases exist.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The hardest part is usually evaluation, not the model call. Engineers used to deterministic software expect to write tests once and trust them, but AI features need a purpose-built eval set, graders that themselves need validating, and constant re-checking, because output quality is a distribution rather than a pass/fail. Without that, every prompt tweak or model upgrade is a blind change, and regressions surface only through user complaints.

Closely related is non-determinism in production: the same input can fail one time in fifty, so debugging requires full tracing of prompts, retrieved context and tool calls, which most teams add too late.

The long tail of real inputs is the next surprise. Demos work on the happy path; real users send ambiguous, adversarial or out-of-scope requests, and getting from 90% to 99% reliability typically takes most of the total effort.

Cost and latency also bite at scale: token spend, rate limits, retries and tail latency force caching, routing and fallback work.

Finally, the ground shifts underneath you: model deprecations and behaviour changes between versions, plus prompt injection and data-leak risks, make maintenance an ongoing cost rather than a one-off build.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Outside engineers typically assume selecting models or crafting prompts is the hard part, when the real operational grind begins after a convincing demo. The steepest hurdle is evaluation and observability: because outputs are probabilistic and open-ended, traditional unit tests cannot catch silent quality regressions triggered by prompt tweaks, upstream data shifts, or subtle provider model updates. Teams end up spending far more time building domain-specific evaluation pipelines curated from real production traces than tuning prompts.

Equally underestimated is context engineering under production constraints—assembling fresh, permission-aware context from messy application state while defending against prompt injection and cross-tenant data leakage. Multi-step workflows also compound tail latency, runaway token costs, and small error rates, since a ninety-five-percent-reliable step chained five times fails nearly a quarter of the time. Finally, handling provider rate limits, brownouts, and model fallbacks without jarring behavioral shifts requires treating inference calls as flaky, stateful dependencies, pairing strict runtime guardrails with product loops that turn implicit user corrections directly into tomorrow’s regression suite.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The hardest part is usually evaluation, not the model. Outside engineers often expect to ship once outputs look good in a demo. In practice, the team has to build its own eval set from real user behavior, set up graders it can trust (human, rubric-based, or model-as-judge, each checked against the others), and rerun everything whenever a prompt, model version, or retrieval index changes. Without that, every change is a guess.

Next comes non-determinism in production. Failures are probabilistic and spread across a long tail, so ordinary monitoring misses them. You need tracing at the level of individual interactions, a way to replay sessions, and feedback loops that turn complaints into regression tests. Upstream model updates can also quietly change behavior when your own code hasn't changed at all.

Cost and latency matter more than people expect. Token use grows with context, agent loops, and retries, so the unit economics and tail latency often look fine in prototypes and then fall apart at scale.

Finally, there's product design for failure: fallbacks, letting users correct the output, setting expectations about what the feature can do, and safety and abuse handling, including prompt injection. Teams tend to treat these as polish to add at the end. They're core infrastructure.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Outside engineers often assume the hardest part of an AI-native feature is getting a compelling prototype to work, when the real operational burden begins after launch. The biggest surprise is usually evaluation: because outputs are non-deterministic and quality is often subjective, shipping even small prompt, retrieval, or model updates requires continuous offline benchmarks and live production monitoring to catch silent regressions. Observability is similarly transformed—standard logs and stack traces cannot explain why a model reasoned poorly, so teams must trace full prompt chains, retrieved context, tool calls, and user corrections to debug failures. Engineers also underestimate the fragility of latency, reliability, and unit economics at scale, where multi-step workflows, long contexts, retries, and upstream provider limits or model deprecations can quickly degrade user experience or invert margins. Finally, managing trust—handling hallucinations, prompt injection, stale data, and graceful failure states—demands tight human feedback loops and ongoing operational ownership rather than one-time implementation.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The hardest part is defining what “good enough” means in a real workflow. A demo can succeed on a handful of examples, while production exposes ambiguous requests, missing context, and plausible answers that are wrong in ways users may never notice. Building representative evaluations takes domain experts, real failure examples, and agreement on which mistakes are tolerable.

The next challenge is containing failures. Teams have to decide when the system should ask for clarification, hand off to a person, or stop before taking an irreversible action. They also need enough tracing to tell whether a failure came from the model, the data it retrieved, or a tool it called. Model updates, changing user behavior, and traffic spikes can shift quality, latency, and cost after launch.

Outside engineers often underestimate how much this depends on people inside the business. Someone has to resolve ambiguous cases, review failures, and own the decision to roll back. That work continues long after the feature ships.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The hardest part is knowing whether the feature still works after you change it. A demo can look convincing even when the model misses the user’s intent, and a fluent wrong answer often looks like a success in the logs. Teams need a way to judge outcomes, a set of cases drawn from real use, and enough tracing to tell whether a failure came from retrieval, the model, or a tool it called.

Engineers also underestimate how tightly reliability, latency, and cost are linked. A retry that improves average accuracy can make the slowest requests intolerable. If the feature takes action on a user’s behalf, a timeout creates a harder question: did the action already happen? Recovering safely requires permission checks, a way to prevent duplicate actions, and a clear handoff when the outcome is uncertain. Much of the ongoing work is turning incidents like these into tests that catch the next regression.
